strengths: Clear motivation shifting focus from subjective believability to objective accuracy in behavior simulation
Real-world e-commerce dataset with 31,865 sessions and 230,965 actions provides valuable resource for process-centric evaluation
Comprehensive evaluation of multiple SOTA models (Claude, Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek-R1) across prompt-only and fine-tuned settings
Clear ablation study demonstrating value of synthesized reasoning traces (e.g., Qwen: 17.26% vs 16.67% without reasoning)
Technically sound methodology with proper train/test splits preventing user session leakage
Well-structured presentation with clear task definition and detailed appendices
weaknesses: Critical limitation: single domain (online shopping) severely constrains generalizability; claims about human behavior simulation broadly are overstated

Synthesized reasoning traces not validated against ground truth; paper admits 'unclear how well the synthesized reasoning trace aligns with human reasoning'; this undermines the entire reasoning augmentation approach
Very low absolute performance (best: 17.26% action accuracy) raises serious practical concerns; inadequate discussion of what this means for real-world deployment
Unfair baseline comparison: prompt-only models have zero domain exposure; no serious attempt to improve prompt-based approaches (better prompts, retrieval-augmentation, etc.)
No human evaluation of synthesized reasoning quality, coherence, or impact on interpretability
Small test set (932 cases, ~2.9% of data) without confidence intervals or significance testing; no per-action-type error breakdown
Limited novelty: core finding (fine-tuning and reasoning help) is expected; contribution is mainly application to action generation task

strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: The distinction between subjective 'believability' and objective 'accuracy' in process-centric human behavior simulation is underexplored and clearly articulated.
Valuable real-world dataset: Large-scale dataset from actual e-commerce platform (31,865 sessions, 230,965 actions) has potential for reproducible benchmarking.
Comprehensive model evaluation: Spans multiple model families (Claude, DeepSeek-R1, Llama, Qwen, Mistral) in both prompt-only and fine-tuned settings.
Includes ablation study: Ablation experiments ('w/o reasoning') provide evidence for reasoning contribution.
Clear presentation: Paper is generally well-written with clear motivation for addressing process-level evaluation gaps.
weaknesses: Unvalidated synthesized reasoning traces (critical flaw): The main methodological contribution lacks human evaluation against ground truth. Paper explicitly acknowledges not evaluating against human-annotated reasoning. Risk of encoding Claude's biases rather than authentic human reasoning. Improvement from reasoning may be confounded with increased training signal rather than reasoning quality. Inconsistent improvements across models (Llama: +6.5pp, Qwen: +0.6pp) suggest instability.

Severely low performance without analysis: Best accuracy is 17.26%, raising fundamental questions about task viability and practical utility. No error analysis, failure mode discussion, or investigation into causes. No evaluation of what percentage accuracy is acceptable for the application domain.

Severe scope limitations: Single task (online shopping), single platform, simplified action space (3 basic operations only). No evidence of generalization. Real web interactions include scrolling, waiting, hovering—all absent. Fundamentally limits claims about 'behavior simulation.'

Insufficient evaluation rigor: Exact match only (no partial credit/semantic similarity). No statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple runs. Only 932 test cases. High variance in 'w/o reasoning' results (9.31%-16.67%) suggests instability. Class imbalance (~95% termination actions) not addressed. Per-class performance not reported.
Unclear action space: Paper doesn't specify total number of possible actions given hierarchical HTML naming, making 17% accuracy difficult to interpret (is it near-random?).

Limited methodological novelty: Fine-tuning LLMs on task-specific data is standard practice. Data augmentation with synthetic examples inspired by prior work. Primarily an empirical study showing unsurprising result (fine-tuning helps).

Missing critical baselines: No comparison with user behavior prediction methods, sequence models (RNNs/Transformers), or simpler statistical baselines. No comparison with related web navigation agents. Improvement over prompting is modest (~5 percentage points).

Reproducibility concerns: Proprietary dataset with vague attribution. Missing details on test/train split methodology, context extraction pipeline, hyperparameter selection, and model sizes. Single epoch training without justification. No code/data release plan.
Reasoning quality not evaluated: No examples of generated reasoning shown. No separate evaluation of reasoning vs. action accuracy. Unknown whether model generates sensible rationales.
No statistical significance testing: No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple runs. Test set size (932) relatively small for reliable estimates.

Large-scale real-world dataset (31,865 sessions, 230,965 actions) from production e-commerce platform
Comprehensive evaluation of multiple SOTA LLMs (Claude, Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen) in both prompt-only and fine-tuned settings
Methodologically sound with proper train/test splits avoiding user overlap and ablation studies demonstrating reasoning importance
Systematic task formulation with clear definitions of context, reasoning, and action components
Demonstrates substantial improvement from fine-tuning (17.26% vs 11.86%) with actionable insights for practitioners
Well-written paper with effective visualizations showing fine-tuned models better match human action distributions
Honest acknowledgment of limitations in Section 6 regarding scope, reasoning validation, and action space
weaknesses: Single-task evaluation limited to online shopping severely restricts generalizability claims; no evidence findings transfer to other behavior simulation tasks (social interactions, UI testing, trust modeling)

Core contribution undermined by unvalidated synthesized reasoning traces: authors explicitly acknowledge 'we have not evaluated on real human-annotated datasets containing authentic reasoning traces'—this is critical since reasoning improvement is a main claim
No human evaluation of reasoning quality despite reasoning being a key contribution; authors admit 'we did not conduct human evaluations on interpretability and usefulness of generated reasoning'
Very low absolute accuracy (17.26%) raises questions about practical utility; no discussion of whether this suffices for real-world deployment or impact on downstream applications
Missing comparisons with non-LLM baselines (RNNs, Transformers, traditional behavior models); unclear if improvements stem from LLM-specific capabilities or just fine-tuning benefits
No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or variance analysis; single-run results without reliability assessment
Oversimplified action space (only 3 actions: click, type_and_submit, terminate) omits scrolling, hovering, waiting—may not capture realistic user behavior

strengths: Makes a valuable distinction between subjective 'believability' and objective 'accuracy' in behavior simulation, addressing an important methodological gap in prior work
Leverages a substantial real-world dataset (31,865 sessions, 230,965 actions) from an e-commerce platform, providing a meaningful resource for reproducible research
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple SOTA models (Claude, DeepSeek-R1, Llama, Qwen, Mistral) in both prompt-only and fine-tuned settings with statistical significance testing
Clear empirical evidence that fine-tuning improves action accuracy by 5.4% and outcome prediction F1 by 13.98% compared to prompt-only methods
Provides actionable error analysis (Figure 3) revealing systematic failure modes, such as ICL models over-generating purchases and struggling with termination decisions
Well-justified design choices for context representation (simplified HTML with hierarchical element naming) that prioritize adaptability and LLM familiarity
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—fine-tuning LLMs on domain data and auxiliary task supervision are standard techniques; the contribution is primarily empirical rather than algorithmic

Critical flaw: synthesized reasoning traces are generated by Claude 3.5 Sonnet but never validated against human reasoning; no human evaluation of whether synthesized reasoning aligns with actual user thinking, making it unclear whether improvements stem from genuine reasoning patterns or artificial auxiliary supervision

Severe scope limitation: evaluation restricted to a single online shopping domain from one e-commerce platform; no evidence that findings generalize to other tasks (web navigation, social interaction, UX testing) despite motivating multiple domains

Statistical rigor issues: test set of 357 sessions (932 cases) is small; sequential actions within sessions are not independent yet treated as separate test cases, violating independence assumptions; no cross-validation, confidence intervals, or multiple runs

Questionable ground truth: models trained to generate synthesized reasoning from LLM-generated examples creates compounding bias risk; if Claude's reasoning contains systematic biases, trained models learn those biases rather than authentic human patterns

Evaluation lacks human assessment: no human judgment of whether generated behaviors appear realistic, and no validation that reasoning explanations are coherent or informative to humans despite claiming to enhance interpretability

Reproducibility concerns: dataset likely non-releasable due to commercial sensitivity (not addressed); no code provided; limited hyperparameter details beyond training setup, preventing independent reproduction

Missing critical comparisons: no ablation on context representation choices, no comparison with other behavior modeling approaches, no domain-specific baselines; limited analysis of what patterns fine-tuned models actually learn

Metric limitations: exact match accuracy for actions is uninformed about error severity (clicking wrong vs. right button treated equally); binary F1 for outcomes is limited; exact match doesn't account for behavioral similarity or partial correctness relevant to simulation

Presentation and framing: title 'Prompting is Not All You Need!' is catchy but misleading—prompting may suffice for believability even if not accuracy; this critical distinction should be prominent; limited qualitative analysis with no example action sequences shown

strengths: Large-scale real-world dataset: 31,865 sessions from an actual e-commerce platform provide a valuable empirical foundation for evaluating behavior simulation
Well-motivated distinction: The paper correctly identifies that 'believability' and 'accuracy' in behavior simulation are orthogonal concerns deserving separate study
Comprehensive model evaluation: Tests multiple SOTA LLMs (Claude, DeepSeek-R1, Llama, Qwen, Mistral) across different sizes and capabilities
Clear task formulation: Well-defined problem with sensible representation choices (simplified HTML, hierarchical element naming, browser-level actions)
Ablation study: Provides evidence that synthesized reasoning traces contribute to performance gains beyond context-action pairs alone

Error analysis: Section 4.6 offers qualitative insights into systematic failure modes (e.g., premature termination, iterative search patterns) and shows fine-tuned models capture more nuanced behavior than prompt-only baselines
Statistical rigor: Reports significance testing (McNemar's test, p-values) for key comparisons
weaknesses: Limited practical impact: Best fine-tuned model achieves only 17.26% action generation accuracy—still unreliably wrong ~83% of the time; outcome prediction at 33.86% F1 raises serious questions about real-world utility and downstream applicability

Unsurprising core finding: Fine-tuning domain-specific models outperforms prompting with no supervision—this is standard machine learning knowledge. The 5.4% absolute improvement over DeepSeek-R1, while statistically significant, is modest and follows predictably from existing work on reasoning models

Methodological flaw with synthetic reasoning: All 'reasoning traces' are generated by Claude 3.5 Sonnet, not actual human reasoning. No human evaluation validates that synthetic traces match authentic user reasoning. The paper acknowledges but does not address the absence of 'real human-annotated datasets containing authentic reasoning traces.' Unclear whether improvements stem from meaningful reasoning or simply additional supervision signal

Severely limited generalization scope: Evaluated on single e-commerce platform only; findings explicitly acknowledged as not necessarily generalizing to other websites or behavioral domains. Single domain evaluation undermines claims about LLM agent capabilities broadly

Weak absolute performance raises fundamental feasibility questions: 17% accuracy means the model fails most of the time. No evidence the fidelity is sufficient for practical applications (UI/UX testing, personalization, agent design). No downstream task evaluation or user studies to validate actual utility

No validation of evaluation metrics: 'Exact match accuracy' is extremely strict and task-insensitive; clicking an adjacent button may be behaviorally similar but counts as complete failure. Per-session averaging is not justified or compared against alternative schemes. Missing essential metrics: end-to-end task success rates, human perception of realism, behavioral similarity measures beyond exact match

Critical reproducibility barrier: Dataset from proprietary e-commerce platform is not released, preventing independent verification or reproduction of results. Insufficient detail on 'cleaned data' process and train/test split strategy beyond user-level separation

Insufficient experimental rigor: (1) Single epoch training with no learning curves or convergence analysis; (2) No data scaling studies to understand sample efficiency; (3) No cross-validation or confidence intervals; (4) Batch size of 1 per device unexplained; (5) No analysis of how context length, session complexity, or dataset size affect performance

Incomplete comparison to baselines: Prompt-only comparisons only use in-context learning; no exploration of other prompting strategies or few-shot approaches. No comparison to supervised sequence models, n-gram baselines, or other behavioral prediction methods from recommendation systems literature

Insufficient analysis depth: Limited investigation of which users/sessions are harder to model; no analysis of action type difficulty hierarchy; no sensitivity analysis on reasoning generation quality; error analysis covers only 3 models. Figure 2 shows distribution alignment but lacks deeper interpretation

Questionable reasoning synthesis process: (1) Dependency on Claude's quality for all reasoning generation; (2) No ablation comparing synthesized reasoning against other supervision strategies (e.g., action-only fine-tuning with auxiliary losses); (3) No diversity analysis of generated reasoning; (4) Potential systematic biases from single-model synthesis unexamined

Missing motivational framing: Paper inadequately establishes why accurate action-level behavior simulation matters. Applications mentioned (UI testing, personalization) are not validated with downstream experiments. No user studies confirm that simulated behavior is useful or predictive

Narrow scope limits contribution weight: Only 357 test sessions (932 test cases)—relatively small test set; single domain and platform; acknowledged uncertainty about generalization; no evidence of transfer to different websites or behavioral contexts

Incomplete related work: Misses connections to sequential recommendation systems, imitation learning, cognitive modeling, and human-computer interaction evaluation literature that address similar behavior prediction problems

strengths: Addresses important gap between subjective 'believability' and objective 'accuracy' in LLM behavior simulation, filling a clear evaluation gap in prior work
Large-scale real-world dataset (31,865 sessions, 230,965 actions) from actual e-commerce platform is significantly more credible than synthetic benchmarks
Process-centric, action-level evaluation is more rigorous than prior work focusing only on final task outcomes
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple SOTA models (Llama, Claude, DeepSeek-R1, Mistral, Qwen) in both in-context learning and fine-tuning settings
Thorough empirical analysis including ablation studies, error categorization, action distribution visualization, and statistical significance testing
Clear findings with strong empirical support: out-of-the-box LLMs achieve ~12% accuracy; fine-tuning improves to ~17%; synthesized reasoning provides further gains
Well-motivated methodology: simplified HTML representation is justified; hierarchical naming practical; reasoning synthesis approach with think-aloud examples is sensible
Actionable insights about behavioral misalignment, including observation that models over-complete vs. under-terminate compared to humans
weaknesses: Limited to single domain (online shopping) and single e-commerce platform; generalizability to other behavior simulation tasks (social interaction, trust games, UI/UX testing) completely unknown, undermining broad claims about LLM agents
Synthetic reasoning traces generated by Claude 3.5 Sonnet are not validated against human reasoning; no human evaluation provided; high risk of introducing model bias into training data
Modest absolute performance (17.26% best action accuracy, 33.86% best F1) raises serious questions about practical applicability; unclear if these results are sufficient for real applications
Small test set of 357 sessions with 932 test cases relative to 230k+ actions dataset; no confidence intervals reported, only p-values; concerns about result stability

Incomplete investigation of why prompting fails; hypothesis about task completion bias mentioned but not rigorously tested; missing ablations on context adequacy, training objectives, or context length
Reproducibility severely limited: proprietary dataset cannot be released, platform identity withheld, no code or model release mentioned—critically limiting for a benchmarking paper
Limited technical novelty: core contribution is standard supervised fine-tuning; reasoning synthesis uses existing LLMs; main novelty is evaluation rather than methodology

Mechanisms of reasoning improvements unclear: is benefit from more training signal or actual reasoning? Inconsistent ablation results (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B: 15.77%→9.31% vs. 1B: 7.53%→11.13%) unexplained
Action space oversimplified (click, type_and_submit, terminate only); missing scrolling, hovering, waiting; may not reflect realistic web interaction
Missing baselines: no comparison to non-LLM approaches (Markov chains, behavior cloning, frequency models); cannot contextualize whether 17% is good/bad
Evaluation metric uses strict exact-match with no partial credit; could mask cases where models generate semantically similar but syntactically different actions
Training/test split not clearly specified; unclear how 31,865 sessions divided or whether stratified; affects reproducibility and validity
Limited exploration of practical applications; UI/UX testing mentioned but not deeply developed; unclear deployment scenarios
